original_question: Which dermatological disorder, first reported by a American dermatopathologist in 1975, is histologically characterized by the same loss of intercellular connections seen in pemphigus vulgaris and absent in bullous pemphigoid?

final_qi.question: Which dermatological disorder, first reported by a American dermatopathologist in 1975, is histologically characterized by the same loss of intercellular connections seen in pemphigus vulgaris and absent in bullous pemphigoid?
final_qi.search_keyword: dermatological disorder 1975 histologically loss intercellular connections pemphigus vulgaris bullous pemphigoid
final_qi.long_answer: Grover’s disease, also known as transient acantholytic dermatosis, was first reported by an American dermatopathologist in 1975. Histologically, it is notable for the loss of intercellular connections (acantholysis), a feature also seen in pemphigus vulgaris but absent in bullous pemphigoid, where the separation occurs at the dermoepidermal junction. Grover’s disease typically presents with pruritic, papulovesicular eruptions and, although its course can be transient, it highlights a unique pattern of intraepidermal acantholytic changes that differentiate it from other autoimmune bullous disorders.

candidate.long_answer: Grover disease, also known as transient acantholytic dermatosis, is a dermatological condition first reported by an American dermatopathologist in 1975. Histologically, it is characterized by acantholysis, which is the loss of intercellular connections between epidermal cells, a feature that is similarly observed in pemphigus vulgaris. In contrast, bullous pemphigoid does not display acantholysis. Clinically, Grover disease typically affects older individuals and presents as a pruritic eruption of papules or vesicles on the trunk. The overlapping histologic appearance with pemphigus vulgaris (acantholysis) makes it distinctive from bullous pemphigoid, where the blister formation occurs without disruption of the intercellular bridges.
